speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF SUMMIT
speechtext: I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister inform the house whether he thinks NATO has been strengthened by the events at the summit conference in Paris.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF SUMMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is not an easy question to answer. I do feel that as a result of the events of the last couple of weeks there has been a greater realization on the part of NATO countries of the need for unity than possibly there has been at any time in recent years. That need of unity has certainly resulted in a new feeling of cohesiveness.
I think I can go no further than that because to do so would simply be to look into the future, but I do express the hope that the various members of the NATO family will emphasize still more the necessity of fuller consultation than ever in the past, for only through full consultation can there be the assurance of that unity which is more necessary today, than it has been for a very long period of time.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF SUMMIT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the Prime Minister tell the house what in particular he proposes to advocate to strengthen NATO militarily during discussions in Washington at the end of this week?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF SUMMIT
speechtext:
The projected meeting between the President and myself will naturally result in discussions taking place between us as heads of friendly nations to the end that the unity that is so necessary in NATO shall be maintained and increased, such unity is indeed so characteristic of our two countries.
[Mr. Benidickson.)

In so far as specific discussions are concerned, I would say that the hon. gentleman will realize that they will cover a variety of matters. I would not be in a position to furnish details-nor would I wish to do so- regarding the agenda which will be before us as we discuss the matters which particularly affect our own countries and international relationships.

wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice. It arises out of a press report headed "B.C. Submits Power Plan for Columbia". In view of the reported announcement on May 31 in Victoria by Hon. Ray Williston, minister of lands and forests, to the effect that British Columbia has offered a complete package deal for the development of the Columbia river, which calls for a storage dam and power plant at the head of the Arrow lakes in the Kootenays; and in view of the fact that the press report indicates that the Times said the plan will bring the federal and provincial governments close to agreement on how to develop the stream; and in view of the minister's clam-like silence on this question, has the minister any information he can properly give the house with respect to this announcement?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fullon (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
thank the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question, of which I also received notice from the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) and other members from the area who are interested in the matter. My attention was drawn to the press report yesterday evening, and in view of its importance I was in touch by telephone with Mr. Williston in Vancouver.
Mr. Williston assures me without reservation that he made no such statement or announcement as is reported in the press. He tells me that what happened was that he was asked by a newspaper correspondent whether it was a fact that what is known as the Arrow lakes dam could be machined and made into a power producer. He confirmed that engineering studies now indicate that that is a possibility. He said that his conversation with the reporter and any definite statement he made went that far only and no further, that he did not announce anything in the way of an offer of a package deal, and that none of the other things attributed to Mr. Williston in the press report originating in Victoria as a statement or announcement of policy, were in fact said by him.

I was glad to have this assurance, which I accept unreservedly. It would, of course, have been a complete departure from the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia with respect to the policy meetings which do from time to time take place between us, had such an announcement been made, because our understanding is that until the whole matter has proceeded to the point where an agreed position is put forward and, we hope, accepted by the international negotiating group, no detailed report or announcement is made. Mr. Williston's assurance given to me yesterday conforms with the letter as well as the spirit of that understanding.
I should perhaps add only by way of additional information, that any suggestion that there was one package deal offered would not have been in accordance with the facts, because as I have told the house on earlier occasions, there are a number of project sequences which have been under discussion. The various considerations with regard to them have been sorted out and examined carefully, and the areas of difference with regard to the approaches to them have been substantially narrowed to the point where it is now sensible for us to hope that a decision as to the best sequence upon which we would most likely reach agreement will be arrived at in the near future.

Hon. Leon Balcer (Acting Secretary of State:) Mr. Speaker, in answer to a question addressed to me by the hon. member for Port Arthur regarding a new companies act, I should like to reply as follows.
A federal-provincial committee on uniformity of company legislation, comprised of the officers of the provincial departments administering the provincial companies acts and the officers of my department who administer the federal Companies Act, has been meeting over the past years with a view to bringing forth companies acts which will be as uniform as possible in all jurisdictions.
Two draft acts have been prepared by this committee, one draft with respect to jurisdictions where incorporation of companies is by means of memorandum of agreement and articles of association, and the other draft where incorporation is by means of letters patent. Representations as to the draft acts have been received from numerous sources such as the institute of chartered accountants, the commercial section of the Canadian Bar Association, the Toronto board of trade and many like professional organizations and individuals.
The conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada is presently in the process of reviewing the two draft acts prepared by the federal-provincial committee on uniformity of company legislation and has appointed two subcommittees, one with respect to the draft act where incorporation is by memorandum of agreement and articles of association and the other with respect to the draft act where the incorporation is by letters patent, for the purpose of putting the language of the draft acts into proper form in accordance with rules of drafting established by the commissioners on uniformity of legislation. This work is presently continuing, a meeting being convened from June 6 to June 10, 1960.
The draft acts prepared by the federal-provincial committee are, of course, available to any interested person who may wish to criticize, comment upon or make suggestions with respect thereto and the draft acts have, in fact, been extensively distributed for this purpose to bodies which include the organizations mentioned from which representations have been received.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton for the second reading of Bill No. C-58, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the close of the debate on this matter yesterday the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) rose and took exception to my having referred to some of the Johnny come lately Conservatives who may not have the same interests as the old-time Conservatives, those who represent the big financial interests. I suggest that by taking this objection to what I was saying he obviously put himself in one camp, and he established which camp that was. Certainly I made no reference to him, and in taking exception he did so of his own volition.
I was pointing out that the present government seems to be trying to do two things at the same time, and I would not be the least bit surprised if two sets of publications should come from government offices with respect to what are the aspects of these amendments. I suggest that in the Financial Post you will probably see press releases over the signatures of government officials indicating that all is well with big business, that big business is going to achieve considerable benefit from these amendments, while at the same time I think we will see in the daily press, which comes in contact with the small retailer, statements indicating that the position of the small retailer is going to be better than it was before.
One particular aspect that has concerned me and certainly has concerned the small business people in my area is the matter of resale


price maintenance. The proposed amendments to section 34 of the act apparently are based on three simple assumptions; first, that the ban on resale price maintenance is fundamentally sound and desirable but, second, that certain practices have developed under section 34 which have been damaging to the small distributor and others and third, therefore the manufacturer should be given the power to restrain such practices by refusing supplies to dealers who engage in them.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, it can be demonstrated that these proposals will effectively eliminate the ban on resale price maintenance; will provide no effective protection, either short or long term, for the small dealer; will open the door to discriminatory practices and strengthen the position of the large distributor who controls private brands, and will place in the hands of the manufacturer a degree of control over the final price of his product that is denied to other groups in the economy. Finally, they are based on a profound misunderstanding of the way in which business is conducted.
Under Bill No. C-58 the supplier merely has to satisfy the court that he had reasonable cause to believe and did believe that certain things were being done and he can then refuse supplies to the parties concerned. We are given to understand by competent legal advice that the test, "had reasonable cause to believe and did believe", is a very vague one and will permit action to be taken by suppliers in such a variety of circumstances as to effectively enforce a thoroughgoing policy of resale price maintenance.
In other fields, Mr. Speaker, we have found' the expression "reasonable cause" not to be effective at all. We have been discussing for a matter of months now the ineffective court procedure in proving reasonable cause. Indeed, it seems probable that in effect parallel but not collusive action to enforce resale price maintenance will be legalized under this amendment which would have been questionable under the combines legislation before section 34 was enacted.
But whatever may be the legal implications of the amendment to section 34, there can be little question but that it is based upon a profound misapprehension of the way business is carried on. Under the proposed amendments the supplier is in effect empowered to refuse supplies on the ground that he had reasonable cause to believe and did believe that the seller was persistently using the article not for the purpose of making a profit thereon but for the purpose of advertising or selling other articles. This suggests that business operates or should operate in the short run in such a way as to obtain a

profit above cost on each individual item it sells. On this issue Howard Clark Green, vice president of the Chicago, Indianapolis and Louisville railway and a financial officer for several other corporations as well as a distinguished accountant, has commented:
Costs influence prices but do not control them. Goods sell for what buyers think they are worth, whether this price is more or less than cost. Business must recover from its total revenues its total costs, but not every sale will show an adequate individual profit. A contribution to overhead is all that can be expected from some classes of business.
Mr. Green continues:
Among the most popular of the notions about fairness in pricing is the idea that a seller is entitled to a price which will cover his cost, plus a reasonable profit.
He then demonstrates the unsoundness of this position and adds:
It is extremely dangerous to assume that the existence of a cost justifies the establishment of a price.
What I have just quoted is found in the "Harvard Business Review", September and October, 1952, page 192. Yet it is precisely this unsound and dangerous principle that the proposed amendments empower a supplier to impose on his distributors. Even if the principle were sound, the practical difficulties encountered in attempting to compute costs and profits for an individual item in the array of items included in a distributor's stocks would be sufficient to rule it out. The problem is made clear in the following quotation from the green book on loss leader selling, a publication of the combines branch:
In some places we have to sell some lines such as butter and shortening with about a 3 to 4 per cent mark-up. Most of our lines are priced at 16 4/16 to 25 per cent, and to tell you the truth I am not able, for the life of me, to tell you what percentage it costs us to handle a pound of butter as against a can of peaches or a dozen of oranges. I know these items represent three different costs in handling, but I do not know, even if we broke our turnover down into each one of the 2,000 items we handle, how we could arrive at a cost for each item.
If, despite its unsoundness in principle and in application, this approach were enacted into law, it seems not unlikely that Canadian courts would follow the same procedure that certain United States courts have adopted in determining when a sale was made below cost. In these cases, statistics compiled by trade associations on the average mark-up for the field in question have been accepted as the cost to be applied to the full range of products in that field. The consequences of such an interpretation would be extremely serious, since it would result in a widening of the distributive margins and probably also in an increase in the numbers involved in distribution-in a word, in an increase in
Combines Investigation Act costs to consumers. It would also appear to be quite legitimate under the proposed amendments for a seller to spend millions on advertising for the purpose of attracting customers to his store, but it would be illegal to pursue and continue a policy of offering specials to do the same thing. The big stores can afford to spend millions, but the small stores cannot.
The small stores would also suffer under the proposed amendments in another way, since on private brands of all kinds the larger stores and chain stores would be free to cut prices to any level they chose, while the small stores handling nationally branded lines would be in danger of having their supplies cut off if they sold at a reduced price which the supplier had reason to believe did not yield a profit for this item.
In questioning a number of stores as to why they did not use loss leaders in certain respects, I asked in particular why Coca-Cola, which could be supplied by a distributor at less than 5 cents, was not used by some of the small stores as a loss leader, especially since the price is considerably higher now. They informed me that if they did there would be no supplies delivered to them. I informed them that if this happened the distributor refusing to supply them would be liable to prosecution. Then the stores pointed out, and quite properly, that this court action could not be instituted by five or six people appealing to the minister to begin an investigation and, subsequently, a court case, but that the retailer himself would have to lay the charge and would have to conduct the court case on his own behalf. As a result, Mr. Speaker, there seldom has been a case in which a small retailer did sell for cost or just above cost when the maintained price was considerably higher, and supplies were discontinued, where he was able to accomplish anything in this field.
I would point out that this was true also in the case of the coal distributors in Timmins. I happen to know the coal distributor who was anxious to eliminate the combine which existed in Timmins. I can tell the house that the one who got hurt the most by the investigation which took place was the distributor who started the investigation as a public service to the community and to the customers in that community. He was the one who got the worst of the whole deal. The combine continued, and his distributors refused to sell to him. The government had no method whatever, or did not use any, to see that he received supplies from his distributors. He had to get back into the combine and agree to sell at a predetermined price or get no supplies. I have seen letters from United States suppliers which definitely stated that unless he was willing to

Combines Investigation Act maintain the price they would not sell any coal to him. This particular individual was almost bankrupt.
In so far as enforcement is concerned under this legislation, it seems clear that those businesses in which trade-ins are common present special problems. Unless some standard system of valuing trade-ins is employed and enforced by a costly system of supervision, the legislation is likely to prove unworkable. Although we consider the legislation unsound in principle, it is manifestly unfair to adopt legislation which will prove to be enforceable in only certain trades. This consideration raises the wider isue as to why the government should empower certain sectors of the economy to enforce prices which will yield a profit over cost while denying the same right to other groups, such as farmers. Again, we consider the principle requiring sales at cost plus a reasonable profit to be unsound and dangerous, but we do not see how the principle can be adopted in one field and denied in others.
There is nothing in the proposed amendments which requires the supplier to uniformly enforce his refusal to supply against all dealers. He may take action against Smith and at the same time permit Jones to continue to sell at the same or even at a lower price. This is subversive of equity and fair dealing. If restrictions are to be enforced they should apply equally to all; they should not be capable of arbitrary, capricious application. Even if a supplier did enforce uniform resale prices based on trade association average mark-up data, the result could still be arbitrary and unwarranted in the case of an individual seller, since the price need not be related to that seller's business experience.
We are fully in agreement with the principle that misleading advertising should be discouraged. Whether such a matter, as well as that of disparaging the quality or price of a product, is not better handled by such organizations as the better business bureaux, is to a considerable degree a matter of opinion. But if legislation on these matters is considered desirable, it is a fact that provision is already made under section 306 of the Criminal Code to deal with misleading advertising at least, and the section could easily be extended to include the aspects of disparagement that it is desired to prohibit. It would be preferable in every respect to make the combines branch responsible for enforcing this section rather than to leave enforcement to the arbitrary decision of suppliers and wholesalers.
We would also question whether loss leader selling, in the sense of selling at below net

invoice cost, is sufficiently widespread to justify extreme measures of the sort proposed in these amendments. The information available in the report of the restrictive trade practices commission on loss leader selling disclosed an extremely limited number of authenticated cases of such sales below cost. No further general survey of the situation has been made available to the public to establish that the situation has undergone any substantial change.
For these reasons, as well as for the more general considerations relating to resale price maintenance which have been fully discussed in the reports of the MacQuarrie committee and of the restrictive trade practices commission, we believe that these amendments are not in the interests in particular of small business, but will tend to create a favourable situation for wholesalers and distributors to the detriment of the small businessman and the consumer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the restrictive trade practices commission report it is stated:
The commission has found that the term "loss leader selling" may be applied by trade groups to any level of pricing, extending from a price in any degree lower than the manufacturer's suggested resale price to a price at or below net purchase cost.
There are exceptions, of course, Mr. Speaker. The report goes on to state:
A merchant may sell goods at or below his net purchase cost to clear end of season or broken lines, to raise money to meet urgent cash requirements, to dispose of discontinued lines of goods and so on. In these and similar cases where the purpose is simply one of disposing of the goods so priced, competitors are not likely to be greatly concerned, although there may be some question at times as to the bona fide nature of the sale and as to the time chosen for making such clearances.
No consideration has been given to those merchants, Mr. Speaker, who operate on a permanent basis under the guise of clearing year end products or the clearance of bankrupt stocks, which are not necessarily bankrupt stocks. We have such establishments in Ottawa and Montreal, what they call war surplus and other surplus disposal establishments, which are not of a temporary nature and where the disposal is on a permanent basis.
Mr. Speaker, we are not particularly worried about big business. I think big business will be able to look after itself. It has all the cards stacked on its side. We have had investigations into a number of what the department considered to be combines and in my opinion we have never yet done anything about those, although they were found guilty. If amendments are going to be made I think they should be amendments that have

some substance. I would suggest that one of those amendments could be in the field of penalties.
First, I think that the clause restricting jury trials is an extremely silly one. I see nothing wrong with jury trials. The minister himself is a lawyer and I am quite sure that if he had a case in which he wanted his client to be well protected, to be given the benefit of the doubt, he would take his case to a jury if it was possible to do so. I am sure the other lawyers in this house-and many of them are defence lawyers-will agree that there is nothing wrong with taking a case to a jury trial.
I would suggest also that the people who are being defended in this case are the small businessmen who are not so well able to look after themselves as they thought they were. They thought that all they had to do was to vote Conservative and they would be well looked after. This is not true. They are not being well looked after. I think they should have the opportunity, when the department decides that there is malpractice in the field of combining, to be represented by jurymen who would sit in judgment on the particular practice that they have before them. I think it is going to be difficult for anybody to argue against a jury.
I expect the minister will rise and say that we cannot have juries because they would not understand the combines legislation. I probably would agree with him that they may not understand it. There are not too many people who do understand it. It is extremely complicated. It is true that the man in the street might not understand it. However, I think the fellow in the street will be interested in what he considers to be a restrictive trade practice. The little fellow working in a garage will know that even in his business there are certain restrictive practices which might be better eliminated for the good of the general consumer. I therefore think little can be said in opposition to a jury trial. If it means that the jury is going to be obliged to ask enough questions to find out just what combines are and what their purpose is and what would be the restrictive practice, then it is all to the good and it will be duly reported in the papers and the general public will get a better understanding of what big business is doing, of what restrictive practices go on.
They may be less lenient in dealing with them than will a judge who in many cases, in my opinion, is closely connected with big business because he is usually associated with big business. He associates with that type of people. He has been associated very likely with corporation law and is sympathetic to
Combines Investigation Act many of the things that are considered to be good, sound business practice. Yet I as a consumer would consider that they were restrictive practices and were tending to increase the cost of the product as it comes down to the consumer.
In the matter of penalties I think we are also extremely foolish. If a gentleman goes into a bank and robs that bank there are a number of penalties that are put against him. Suppose he gets $10,000 and walks out of that bank. First of all, the law will try to get the $10,000 back if it can. Then the man will be put in jail and even the penalty of a fine may be imposed on him; but the law will get back, if possible, that amount of money. What manner of thinking do we have when we allow a business to make, we will say, as the combine investigation into sugar pointed out, terrific amounts of money, up in the millions, and then if we convict them we would likely have imposed a penalty of $10,000?

The official opposition has ignored the fact that this bill is supposed to give some badly needed assistance to the small businessman and the points which have been raised are nothing more than historical rhetoric and technical arguments to conceal the fact that this legislation is intended to help the small businessman. They seek in turn to prove that the Liberal party was right in 1951.
I have not been able to discover what is exactly the attitude of the C.C.F. group. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who spoke last night and again today, gave me the impression that he was speaking in favour of the bill. He certainly adopted a good many of the arguments that I had intended to raise, namely the very difficult position of small businessmen and the difficulties they have with big business. However, I regret I lost the thread of his argument, and I really did not discover the grounds on which he feels he must oppose the bill. I might go into the arguments he raised in connection with the legal aspect of jury trials but frankly I do not wish to be diverted. I would only say that most of the arguments he put forward in connection with jury matters were definitely wrong in the light of jurisprudence established for many years.
A short summary of the bill is that it is an attempt to bring some balance into the complex and difficult subject of trade practices. The bill is not weighted against big business, nor against small business, nor against the consumer. Yet to each of them it gives some benefit which they have been needing and demanding. The opposition have taken one part of the bill-the part which deals with what I consider the perfectly proper agreements between manufacturers- and have attempted to show that the bill as a whole is in favour of big business. The opponents of this measure have, generally speaking, completely ignored at least three other parts which I will discuss later and which are very much in favour of the small businessman.
It is surely unnecessary to say that the retail merchants associations, and small business across Canada, have been asking for legislation such as is now proposed for their own protection, particularly with reference to loss leader sales. I have a great many such requests in my office, and I am sure other hon. members have received petitions of this kind. I have one in my hand now which I think requests exactly what the hon. minister has proposed in this present


bill. It is dated April 28, 1960, and I will quote it in part. Urging support of this legislation, it says:
These issues are of vital concern to the vast majority of independent retailers, and we urge you and the government to take the necessary action at this session of parliament to eliminate loss leaders, predatory price cutting, discriminatory pricing practices, false advertising; and to enact legislation to aid small business.

The letter is dated April 28. However, I am sure it did not refer to this bill. It is a request that the government introduce legislation to eliminate loss leaders, predatory price cutting, discriminatory pricing practices, false advertising, and legislation to aid small business.
I was pointing out that what these people ask is exactly what is included in this bill. I think every item requested in this particular letter is there. This particular letter appears to be a printed form issued by the merchants' association. I have the names, and I am quite prepared to disclose them. This is the kind of petition which members of the house have been receiving. I am sure most hon. members have received them, and they do ask for just about what the government has now proposed. I believe it would deal a death blow to many small businesses right now if they were denied the benefit of some protection against loss leader selling. This is one thing which has been proposed to me time and time again by small businessmen. This is what they believe is causing them trouble. They believe it is discriminatory and that it is gradually putting them out of business.
In proposing this legislation the government has almost entirely answered the request which small business has made, and in these circumstances it is beyond my understanding why both opposition parties should have taken such a strong stand with regard to this bill, the strongest stand which has been taken, I think, on any bill during the four sessions I have been here. Spokesmen for the parties have said they would fight this bill to the bitter end, but for the life of me I have heard no reason given which would justify the opposition being so intense.
I should like to discuss for a few moments what the objections have been. In my opinion the objections raised have been very shallow indeed. To deal, first of all, with the section relating to combines, this is, to my mind, the

first example of an attempt to bring balance into combines legislation. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has stated that the courts will not be able to interpret the act properly. He has said that the courts will give a broader interpretation to the exemptions detailed under the act than they should. He has said that under the guise of the exemptions granted the courts will give a much broader interpretation of the legislation than they now do. To this I say that we must rely on the ability of our courts and judges to determine what the clear wording of this clause means. I do not think we can go on the assumption that there will be difficulty in doing so. We must not assume that all persons accused under this clause will be acquitted merely because certain defences are enumerated in the bill. While certain defences are allowed, the final provision makes definite prohibition against price cutting agreements.
I should like to say just a word about the history of combines legislation. The Leader of the Opposition tried to show that the Conservative party, historically, was reluctant to enact combines legislation or to enforce it. I should like to make three points which, I think, definitely refute this allegation. As was pointed out by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) yesterday, the original anti-combines section which was placed in the Criminal Code was enacted by the Conservative government in 1889. The Combines Investigation Act of 1910, which was brought in by a Liberal government, revealed two prime weaknesses, and those weaknesses were subsequently corrected in the Conservative legislation of 1919. In this case I should like to refer to the MacQuarrie report issued in 1952. At the top of page 12, in referring to the 1919 Conservative legislation, the report reads:
It is to be observed that the legislation overcame two of the principal defects of the act of 1910, namely the absence of a continuing enforcement authority and the initiation of investigations only on the application of interested private individuals.
Further down, in referring to the 1923 legislation, the report states:
The Combines Investigation Act of 1923 followed. The act was basically the act as it stands today. The comprehensive definition of "combine" of the legislation of 1919 was largely retained but no administrative power to order the cessation of activities was provided for.
Now, as some hon. members may point out, the legislation of 1919 was declared ultra vires because it provided for certain administrative matters which the privy council felt were beyond the authority of parliament. Nevertheless, as is pointed out in the report, when the 1923 act was re-enacted the main provisions of the Conservative act
Combines Investigation Act of 1919 were reincorporated, and this legislation has carried through until the present time. The basic change from that was that the provisions which offended against the privy council decision were removed in the 1923 act. But basically we have the 1889 act as legislation of the Conservative government and the 1919 legislation of the Conservative government, which form the main foundation of our present act.
I think it would be a fair statement to say that combines legislation has been a progressive development undertaken seriously by governments of both parties, and I think it would be quite wrong to say that either party has taken the lead or lagged behind in progress on combines legislation.
I should like to turn to the price maintenance portion of the bill. In his remarks the Leader of the Opposition stated that under this bill the manufacturer or supplier will be in a position to refuse to sell his products to an outlet for some vague reason and on some indefinite report which he has received. This particular statement was made time and time again by members of the opposition party who said, the manufacturers are going to make nonsense of this because they are going to be cutting off retailers for no reason at all. Will the manufacturer of any product be over-anxious to cut off his retail outlets for an unreasonable excuse? I think not. I think every manufacturer is anxious to retain as many retail outlets for his products as he can, and I believe it would be only in the case where some retailer was outrageously making a breach of the loss leader rules, and the other things which are mentioned in the act, that the manufacturer would ever move in and cut off the retailer. They are in business; they want to have outlets, and they will not cut them off unless they have a perfectly good reason.
In my opinion this is another example of balance in the combines legislation. The 1951 legislation went from one side to the other; it went from one swing of the pendulum to the other, and in eliminating one danger they created another one just as great.
The Leader of the Opposition also said that we have no interest in the consumer; that the Minister of Justice hardly mentioned him; that the provisions of the legislation left the consumer hanging in the balance. I say two things. First, if the small businessman is put out of business by such tactics as loss leader selling and various of the other unfair trade practices mentioned in this act which are prohibited, then the consumer is left in the hands of big business, and I am sure we would agree that this is not at all satisfactory. Just to give some verification of my statement, I should like to read from the
4424	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act report of the royal commission on price spreads on food products, which makes this very clear. Volume 1 of the report of the royal commission on price spreads of food products, September, 1959, at page 59, states:
We have pointed out that we have been unable to discover evidence to support the view that the increase in the size of the large firms in the food industries, which has accompanied the general expansion of the market, has resulted in reduced costs and a tendency to reduce prices to consumers. We are disposed to explain this partly in terms of the tendency for large firms to compete in offering services rather than reduction in prices. We find no substantial basis to suppose that, if the major firms in the food industries continue to increase in size, this will operate in the direction of reducing prices to consumers.
Second, does the consumer really benefit from these loss leader sales? I doubt this very much. The report from which I have just read indicates that loss leader sales are "come on" gimmicks to bring people into the stores. Large businesses or small businesses have to make a profit, and if they take a loss on one item they must sell something at a higher price to make up for it.
The basic design of this bill, as I see it, is unashamedly to give a break to the small businessman. He does not want subsidies or loans or charity so much as he wants fair competition. The small businessman knows that the big dealer can buy cheaper in quantity lots; that he can afford larger advertising costs, and that he can stand a smaller margin of profit on volume sales. He knows this; he knows he has to deal with it, and most of them have said that they can deal with it; that they can meet this competition if they are given a fair break on trade practices. They cannot meet discriminatory and unfair trade practices which are forced upon them and upon the public by the big business operation.
In this bill there are three main provisions to help the small businessman. First, there is the elimination of the abuses of loss leader selling; second, there is the elimination of false advertising, which not only swindles the consumer but loses legitimate sales for the legitimate businessman. Third, it eliminates discriminatory promotional rebates, which are granted on a different basis from one person to another. I should like to deal with them in the order I have mentioned.
I think that the legislation of 1951, by which price maintenance was prohibited, went too far. Not only that, the report on which this legislation was based indicates the dangers of loss leader selling.
Undoubtedly there were and are dangers in resale price maintenance. The consumer does not secure the benefit of wholesale competition in retail buying, according to the


proponents of the 1951 legislation, but they either failed to observe or underestimated the dangers of loss leader selling which have become more obvious in recent years. It is doubtful, as I have said before, if the consumer really gains anything and it is very devastating for the small businessman. He cannot buy in huge quantities like the chain stores, nor can he afford to lose money on various items and hope to recoup his loss from others. Under the present law neither the wholesaler nor his supplier can help him out if he gets into difficulties on loss leader selling. They are forbidden from taking any action of a restrictive kind against those engaged in loss leader selling and selling products to the detriment of their regular dealers is something that is constantly carried out.
The present bill gives the manufacturer the right which he so badly needed in the 1951 legislation. If the report on which the 1951 legislation was based had been followed I think that some such provision would have been included. It certainly is indicated but in fact no such release valve was provided. They merely went from resale price maintenance to no resale price maintenance and left small business in the difficulties that now face it.
Some mention has been made of the Mac-Quarrie report in connection with loss leader selling. This is a report of the committee to study combines legislation. I should like to quote from pages 70 and 71 to indicate the dangers which were then pointed out to the government relating to loss leader selling. Paragraph 7 on page 70 reads as follows:
Resale price maintenance no doubt helps to protect the reputation of branded goods and facilitates advertising and sales promotion. However, the committee is not convinced by the argument that the reputation of branded goods greatly suffers from normal price variations and that people will think quality has deteriorated if prices are allowed to vary. If the loss leader is taken care of, normal price reductions will not cause serious problems to the manufacturer.
In the same report, under "general conclusion and recommendations", there is the following:
As to the loss leader device, the committee believes that it is a monopolistic practice which does not promote general welfare and therefore considers that it is not compatible with the public interest.
Those are the observations made in the report, on the basis of which the 1951 legislation was carried into effect. I think what we are doing now is belatedly putting these loss leader restrictions into the act in a manner in which they undoubtedly should have been put into the act when the previous legislation was passed.
I should like to discuss two other matters in the bill concerning which there has been very little discussion up to this time. The

first has to do with misleading advertising. This is something that has long been deplored by the general public and dealers both large and small. Certain types of individuals, groups and companies who have inserted themselves into the economy have sent out catalogues, leaflets and other advertising material which has been false in some of its aspects. The particular item with which the bill deals is misrepresentation of the price at which certain articles are normally sold to the public. I think it is agreed generally that it would be impossible for anyone to prohibit by legislation exaggerated claims as to the value of an article. From time immemorial in business dealings people have exaggerated the value of the article they were selling beyond what they should have. It is a very common expression that a certain article is a bargain at twice the price. Those prospective purchasers who are gullible may be taken in but those who are not will not be, no matter how glib the seller. No legislation could ever prevent that.
But if a consumer is given what he believes to be a fact on which he makes his judgment and that fact is false, then his judgment in the matter has been completely perverted. If he is told that an article is normally sold at a certain price and that is not the fact then he may be improperly swindled into buying an article which is not worth what it is stated to be, never was and never will be.
I admit I have some doubts as to the enforcement of this provision. Proof as to what the ordinary price is or has been may be very difficult to give. This seems to me to be something that the courts will have to deal with and those conducting prosecutions will have to be very careful about it. However, I believe it will dispose of the most flagrant cases of fraudulent misrepresentation of the value of goods, and to that extent I am sure it will be valuable. The general efficiency of the provision about false advertising will have to be proved in the light of experience.
The third and final matter in the bill which is designed to help small business is the restriction on promotional allowances and rebates. This is a type of indirect price reduction which the small dealer cannot secure from the supplier or the manufacturer but which the larger corporations such as chain stores can force from the supplier. This provision does not prohibit reductions for quantity purchases. There again I think there would be no hope or expectation of refusing to a person who can buy in large quantities a substantial discount compared with the person who must buy in small quantities. Those are normal trade difficulties that
Combines Investigation Act the small businessman must deal with. However, this particular provision does not deal with a reduction for quantity purchasing but has to do with a sort of squeeze play which is imposed on the supplier by the large buyer. This practice is given considerable attention in the report of the royal commission on price spreads in 1959 and in the report of the restrictive trade practices commission on the grocery trade in 1958. I should like to read from page 180 of the latter report on the grocery trade to give the house some idea of the type of promotional rebate which is considered discriminatory. At the bottom of page 180, it is stated:
The most pernicious form of rebate that is currently required by chain stores is that of "promotion allowance". Before any of the large chains will give special display space to a product, they insist on a payment that can run as high as $75 per store per week. Some chains will refuse to stock an item unless a prior commitment of "promotional advertising" is made by the supplier.
Conditions have reached the stage whereby "promotion allowances" are the competitive weapons used by competing suppliers-and the method employed is equivalent to nothing more or less than hidden discounts.
It is obvious, therefore, that from the supplier's point of view he is being gradually forced to "rent" space for his product on the shelves of the large chain stores. No independent would dare ask for such an arrangement and therefore being without this source of income is once again at a competitive disadvantage with the chain store.
If this type of unfair trade practices is present, the bill provides that such allowances must be offered on proportionate terms to all purchasers from all individual manufacturers or suppliers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I cannot for the life of me see how the opposition can make such a strong stand in connection with this very beneficial provision for the small businessman. The manufacturer is given the right, under this bill, to engage in legitimate agreements which will have the effect of cutting down cost of production and thus reducing the price; the small businessman, is given a measure of protection against unfair competition; the consumer benefits from reduced costs, honest advertising, and the tremendous benefit which small business brings to the economy.

Mr. Speaker, I was deeply interested by the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). I know that he tried very hard to convince the house and the nation that the Conservative party had done more than anyone in Canada in applying the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. However, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the member for Hull (Mr. Caron) showed that the Liberal party had introduced the

Combines Investigation Act amendments without which the act was inefficient and inoperative. It was in fact under a Liberal regime that many people and companies were indicted for offences under the act.
I was a bit surprised to hear the member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) say just now that the Liberals have little interest in the small businessmen, the little fellow.
If he will just listen to me for a few minutes, I can tell him that in 1955 I asked for an investigation to protect not the powerful but the little fellow, in my constituency, my province and my country. And it was the Liberal party that authorized such an investigation, which unmasked the most powerful monoply in Canada, namely the pulp monopoly.
Speaking in this house, on January 14, 1955, I described the situation of the settler and the farmer who were being exploited by the large paper companies. The L'Union Catholique des Cultivateurs de Quebec and representatives of farmers' co-operatives in my constituency had asked me to demand an investigation to stop the exploitation then going on in my constituency. At the time, I told the house that in 1951, companies buying fir and spruce, the pulp woods grown in my constituency, paid the farmers and settlers $15 a cord, delivered to the Gatineau or Lievre river, while they sold the newsprint at $101.48 a ton at the mills.
In 1952, the same companies lowered the price of pulpwood to only $14.50, while they raised the price of newsprint to $105.22 a ton.
In 1953, the same companies were paying settlers and farmers only $13.50 a cord for pulpwood, while newsprint sold at $110.05 a ton.
In 1954, the same companies paid $13.50 a cord and sold their newsprint at $110.03 a ton.
Having found that while newsprint prices were going up, the prices paid to settlers and farmers for the raw material used in newsprint manufacturing were declining, I therefore demanded an investigation.
1 concluded my remarks by asking for an investigation. This is what 1 said, as recorded on page 215 of Hansard for January 14, 1955:
This is why I am asking the Minister of Justice to start an investigation immediately, under the Combines Investigation Act, on the operations of the E. B. Eddy, of Hull, the Canadian International Paper, whose head office is in Montreal, and the James MaeLaren's, of Masson.


A few days after, other Quebec and New Brunswick members, putting forward the same reasons, asked for an investigation in their area. A week after that request, the then minister of justice, Mr. Garson, stated in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Labelle that the investigation was under way, since he had instructed the director of combines investigation to launch an inquiry, under the Combines Investigation Act, regarding companies of the province of Quebec, of eastern Ontario and even of New Brunswick.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of my remarks I want to commend and congratulate the director of combines investigations and the other members of the commission for the tremendous job they have done. They worked most intelligently for the success of their inquiry and in preparing the report submitted to the Minister of Justice. After examining that report, the Minister of Justice prosecuted the corporations, and today, I would like to commend the Minister of Justice as well as the government for the action taken.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention to read the whole report on that investigation. It is extremely interesting, but I would like to quote at least an excerpt of the concluding remarks, because it must be understood that the inquiry on paper firms differs from other investigations. Ordinarily, corporations form a combine in order to establish fixed prices to the buyer, and in the present case, the companies agreed to fixed prices to the producer.

I appreciate this, Mr. Speaker, and you are right. I only want to quote a short excerpt of the report and shall link the whole with my concluding remarks. In paragraph 2, chapter 4 of the report, we can read this:
The arrangements made to offer certain prices for farmers' pulpwood can be considered as pricefixing arrangements, for the maintenance of the prices that the farmers could get for their pulpwood. If the situation most frequently encountered

in the application of the Canadian anti-combines act involved the fixing of sale prices by suppliers, such restrictive effects may result from an arrangement made to fix purchase prices by buyers whose total purchases are large in relation to the total purchases of a given area.
It was clearly stated in the former act that companies were not allowed to make arrangements to fix prices; in fact, the learned lawyers of the large companies tried to prove to the combines investigation commission that when they had meetings of 10, 12, 15 or 20, they had not discussed prices, stating that they had not met for the purpose of fixing prices, but only to obtain information and statistics of possible benefit to them.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what do we find in the suggested amendments to this bill? What is the meaning of section 32? It is quite simple, this section will legalize the meetings where statistics, research and everything will be discussed. When this bill is adopted, the combines investigation commission will no longer be able to clearly establish evidence against those companies which have combined, because I may assure you that in future, minutes of such meetings will no longer be published as they were in the past. Now it was on the basis of the minutes and letters written after those meetings, by representatives who had been present at the meetings that the director succeeded in proving there had been a combine. However, due to the amendments that are suggested to the present section, the director will no longer be able to prove that the companies have met, discussed together and made arrangements.
Therefore, instead of improving the act, as contended by the Minister of Justice, this amendment is bound to make it less efficient. Not only will the act be less efficient, but another, much farther reaching and more dangerous amendment is introduced. Under the act as it now stands, companies found guilty of a first offence are subject to a fine, while for a second offence the attorney general may sue both the company and the directors, and have either a fine or a prison term imposed by the court.
Now in the amendment put forward under section (4) of clause 17, here is what we find:
In any case where subsection (2) of section 31 is applicable the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of the province may in his discretion institute proceedings either by way of an information under that subsection or by way of prosecution.

Mr. Speaker, I think that most of us in this house agree that the old act was not adequate. It was unsatisfactory. However, in our opinion, the amendments now offered will make the act even less acceptable to the interests of Canadian individual free enterprise and also less acceptable to all those who are concerned with the welfare of the Canadian consumer.
It is our opinion in this group that we are living today under economic anarchy and that free enterprise no longer exists. Any attempt on the part of any political party to take political advantage by paying tribute to so called free enterprise is spurious, in the first instance, because free enterprise has already disappeared. We have economic anarchy and nothing less.
I maintain that we have in office now a government which admits that the old Combines Investigation Act is ineffective and is now offering amendments which will completely eliminate the little bit of effectiveness which exists in the law as it is now on the statute books. I can remember very well how the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) rose in his place when he was in the opposition and complained about the ineffectiveness of the existing legislation. He used to demand that there ought not to be the option of a fine but that any officials of a corporation found guilty of violations of the act ought to be forced to serve a prison term.
What the minister is now offering the house is a far cry from the demands made by the Prime Minister when he was a leading member in the opposition ranks in this house. The minister, in effect, is now asking the house

Combines Investigation Act to agree to a lessening of restraints and conditions and opening the door wide to the exploitation of the consumers in the interests of the monopolies, and incidentally at the expense of the only free enterprises which are left in our nation today.
We are to an increasing degree living under a controlling economy. Whether we like it or not I think most of us have to recognize this basic assumption. However, in our group we are concerned not so much with the inevitable; we are concerned with the problem that if we have to live under a controlling economy, who are the people who are going to do the controlling? Apparently the minister is perfectly happy to aid and abet the controls so that they end up in the hands of the few people who are responsible not to the consumers of Canada but only to the vested interests they represent.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record part of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) of April 9, 1959. On page 2408 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
No review of the economic situation would be complete without some comment on price movements. In the fourth quarter of 1958 consumer prices were 2.4 per cent higher than a year earlier. The wholesale price index rose 1.3 per cent in the same period. This tendency toward rising prices, particularly in a period of recession, is a matter for concern. Advancing technology might have been expected to reduce the cost and selling price of many products to consumers. It is evident, however, that developments in corporation pricing policies, in labour organization and even in our political democracy are producing increased rigidities which inhibit the free play of competitive forces and thereby promote inflation and price increases.
In the light of that admission on the part of the Minister of Finance a little over a year ago it is our contention that the fines now imposed under the existing legislation are a farce indeed. The offerings of the government by way of amendments are really ridiculous and a cruel hoax on the small businessmen of our nation. We have many organizations who have made representations in regard to this legislation, and I agree with most of the motions of local chambers of commerce and boards of trade. However, I should like to underline the fact that the national organization representing the businessmen present a viewpoint that is alien to the interests of the small and independent businessmen of the nation today. Our national chamber of commerce represents in effect the identical interests of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I know that many local chambers of commerce and boards of trade do not realize how they are misrepresented by their national organization when it makes its annual presentation to the government.

They are completely dominated by the vested interests, by the big outlets. The small businessmen, while they may be members of the local board of trade or the local chamber of commerce, and even though the whole of this movement may express ideals which are completely in line with the national interest, are completely betrayed at the national level when the national organization makes its representations to our cabinet.
We are concerned about the survival of the individual in our society. When the last election rolled around, the Conservatives were very prolific in the tears they shed on behalf of the independent businessmen of Canada. What have they done since they assumed office some three years ago? It is our conviction that they have done nothing which would help in any way to assure the survival of the independent small businessman. The legislation now before the house is a smoke screen, and there is nothing in it which would really and effectively help small business to survive. We have had the estimates of the government before us over a period of years. We once noticed in the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) a vote of $30,000 to establish a branch devoted to the interests of small businessmen. That is not even enough to establish a filling station in my riding. It is nothing-peanuts. We realize, too, that in the estimates this year there is nothing so far as the small businessman is concerned. If the government makes any pretence at all that the legislation now offered is going to help the small businessman-and I notice the minister did so the other day-the government is misinformed, because the legislation now before us is going to do nothing which will be of any assistance. As a matter of fact, it will do a lot of harm to the long term survival of the small businessman in Canada.
About a year ago the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) outlined in this house a number of proposals whereby the capital needs of small business might be supplied. The house turned a deaf ear to those proposals at the time. Our movement has always been concerned with the survival of the individual as an individual in our society. As the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) emphasized on that occasion, our movement originated because of our concern with the importance of the individual.
I have a number of letters here which I should like to read into the record in order to highlight what is happening. I have one from a man by the name of A. F. Maley. His address is 283 Somerset street east, Ottawa, and he says:
Subject: The United States monopoly of car polish. How they get it and the remedy.

Bennett took it up some 25 years ago-
I assume the writer is referring to the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.
*-and after investigating reached an agreement with the oil company that each service station operator he classed as an independent dealer in accessories, and that the oil companies put up a dealer sign over the doors of the service station.
I am going to confine my remarks to the polish industry but the same applies to accessories in general. It resulted in many Canadian polish factories opening up in Canada owned and controlled by Canadians.
But when the Liberals came into power the dealer signs came down and lessee signs went up enabling the major oil companies to write in the leases that the station operators would henceforth buy their accessories from the oil companies or from distributors appointed by the oil companies.
In Ottawa, oil company representatives canvassed the distributors telling them that they had to pay payola of around 5 per cent to have their firms classed as company approved dealers.
I will not read the rest of the letter. However, this kind of thing is happening on a wide scale today. The oil companies are dictating to the retailers as to where they must buy their anti-freeze, their spark plugs, their tires and other accessories. The rake-off, or the payola, in a great many instances exceeds the normal retailer's margin, and it is a crime. The officials who are guilty of this kind of practice are, in my books, more guilty of a crime against society than is an unemployed man who, in order to help out his dependants and assure them of their daily bread, robs a grocery store. I have no sympathy at all for these officials and, like the Prime Minister when he sat in the opposition, I say that the officials of these companies are criminals acting against the interest of the Canadian public. They are fleecing the Canadian people, and they should not have the option of paying a fine. They should be confined behind bars in order that they might receive an education behind bars as to what their responsibilities to society ought to be.
I have another letter here. This is a letter from the reeve of the township of Thorold, who lives in Allanburg, Ontario. It is addressed to my house leader and reads:
Dear Hazen:
A local wholesale electrical distributor in the Welland district is the victim of a combine by the other distributors. It has reached the point where he will probably be put out of business because the manufacturers will no longer sell to him.
I am enclosing a copy of his letter.
And so on. He asks my house leader to do what he can to ensure the survival of this independent business operator. The letter that is written by the manager of the firm -I assume it is the manager-an R. Smith, to the reeve, says:
As we have been fortunate enough in spite of pressure from the larger distributors to gradually 79951-0-279J
Combines Investigation Act
gather lines on the direct basis from manufacturers it seems that we are giving our opposition some fair competition and apparently they do not like it.
I have heard that at the last meeting of Canadian electrical distributors association that they are going to put me out of business by as a group telling the manufacturers that unless they stop selling to me they will refuse to buy from them.
I would appreciate any help or suggestions that you may have in order to fight this combine.
I feel that the legislation now offered is not going to help the interests of the real Canadian individual engaged in business. I hold in my hand a bottle of Car Slick cleaner and polisher. This was put out by a manufacturer in Montreal who used to do a business of $100,000 a year and who supplied employment to Canadians. However, because his product was not acceptable as far as the oil companies were concerned, he was run out of business; he had to close up. I am afraid that Conservatives are not very interested in the survival of small business because there is nothing in the legislation now offered that I can see that will help to ensure the survival of the small businessman.
As the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) underlined last night, the government of the day is attempting to sit on both sides of the fence. It does not want to hurt monopoly business; it does not want to invite the antagonism of big business. In our opinion, the legislation now offered is not going to invite the antagonism of big business; it is going to invite the support of big business. Yet, at the same time I know the government is going to make every effort to assure the small businessman that they have made an attempt to ensure his survival. You cannot have it both ways.
Recently I have had many invitations to speak to organizations of small businessmen. I am advising them that unless they organize politically and economically, under the existing regime they have little hope for survival. The only hope available is that the good Lord helps those who help themselves. They have to realize that their interests lie in teamwork, the one with the other, and they have to battle the monopoly interests that exist.
Any argument that big business is in the interests of consumers is completely fallacious because, as the royal commission report on price spreads emphasizes, if he is given a reasonable break the small businessman can outmanoeuvre the large business any day of the week. He can survive. However, unfortunately he is not being given a reasonable break under present conditions. If we are to allow the continuous disappearance of the small businessman in our nation eventually the consumer is going to pay, and he is going to pay very heavily.

Combines Investigation Act
We see happening in the business world what is happening in agriculture. We see vertical integration, and I regret that there are many wholesale houses today that issue to the corner store not one price list, but a price list containing categories A, B, C and, out in British Columbia, categories D and E, and the margin between categories A and E is wider than the normal retail market margin. In addition to A, B, C, D and E, there are the normal discounts for purchases on a volume basis. Whether or not you are in category A, C or E depends on whether you take your whisky at the same country club as the owner of the wholesale house. This, I feel, is most unfair and it ought to be looked into.
I agree that there ought to be some discounts for purchases on a volume basis. However, there ought not to be any discount because of your relationships with the manager of the wholesale house or the manufacturer. I regret that our society has not paid very much attention to the increasing growth of what I would like to call the managerial class in our society. You know, an ethical argument is often presented-and I admit, with validity-on behalf of ownership. However, in our society today we have a new class, namely the managerial class, which has little ownership and little personal interest except the interest of self-advancement, and this often works against the interests of the consumer.
The managerial class also works against the interests of ownership. In increasing degree ownership is unable to have a determining voice. There was a day when we held ownership responsible and under certain conditions ownership would respond to the needs of society. You have, for instance, the Rockefeller Foundation and so on. However, today ownership means nothing; management means all. This legislation does nothing whatsoever to curtail the ambitions of management as opposed to the interests of either the consumers or ownership. The answer offered by the minister amounts to nothing as far as the survival of the small businessman is concerned.
I know that the retail merchants association has asked for the re-establishment of resale price maintenance. However, when they met us even the retail merchants association agreed that the public interest should receive some consideration if we re-established price maintenance legislation and legalized the practice. There is nothing in the legislation whatsoever that will protect the interests of the consumer. In our opinion the minister is simply opening the door wide, and even though we regret the lack of effectiveness of the old legislation the new legislation will

assuredly be found less effective except in one respect. It will mean that the lawyers of the nation will make millions of dollars. They are going to have a real field day with the proposed legislation. The old legislation was weak enough but with the new legislation it will be years before the first test case is finally settled. In the meantime the lawyers will have made hundreds of thousands of dollars and the consumers will have received nothing.
The government hopes it can assure big business that it has done nothing that might hurt their aspirations. At the same time the government hopes to be able to mislead "ma" of the corner store into believing that her interests have been looked after. I have great respect for "ma" at the corner store and I am very anxious to see her survive because at a late hour in the evening or on a holiday what do we do when we need milk, bread, any other essential or even a non-essential item? We knock on the door and "ma" who has an apartment above the corner store comes down and opens the store and gives you your bread or milk or butter. "Ma" is being squeezed out of business, and the government is aiding and abetting the monopoly interests in squeezing her out of business through the amendments they are now presenting to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of years the small businessmen and merchants have been asking the government to give them some assistance and protection. They have seen other aspects of our economy being assisted in one way or another, through deficiency payments and so on. Their voice has been a voice in the wilderness. They have not been given the attention that they consider necessary in view of their position in the economy of Canada. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) stated to the house in his speech that the present act was satisfactory and that the only changes that needed to be made were a few in respect of administration. I would therefore assume, by implication, that he felt that the small businessmen had been adequately protected by that act.
The Liberals were warned in 1951, when this amendment was put into effect, that it would not protect the small merchants. However, the Liberals were deaf to the call and to the warning. Today, when the government has brought forward this amendment in the hope of giving some assistance to the small businessmen, the Liberals are still deaf to the call. They think that all is well. The fact that retail merchants and several businessmen across the country have been asking that something be done means little or nothing to them. So far as they are concerned the act is perfect in its application and in its design.
The problems, of course, of the small businessmen in this changing and growing economy are varied and have many implications. The small businessmen who are along what we call the ribbon business areas, are not only plagued by competition of this type at
Combines Investigation Act which the legislation is aimed, but they are also plagued by local problems, such as parking or competition from shopping plazas and so on. The particular problem we have before us today is a problem for which they asked for some relief, some assistance and some protection. As to whether or not the act, as amended, will meet all the requirements, time alone will tell. In dealing with matters of economic law it is like dealing with the laws of nature. When one makes a change one is not quite sure of its implications.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, m respect of these amendments, that if the purpose of the amendments is not fulfilled I am sure the government's mind would be open to changes which might be necessary in the future to fulfil that purpose. However, I feel the government should be complimented upon at least listening to that voice and attempting to make some change.
Liberal speakers, including the Leader of the Opposition have tried to maintain the myth that they are the champion of the little businessmen; that they are the champion of these men against big business. They neglected to point out what history has shown, that this party also has taken steps and passed legislation to limit the activities of combines. The Leader of the Opposition implied that the Conservative party was the party that intended to leave free enterprise alone, without any interference. Of course he forgot to mention that it was Liberalism that adopted this laissez-faire course. They have forgotten Conservative attempts to organize such things as the Ontario Hydro, when it was necessary to protect hydro development, and also the creation of the Canadian National Railways. These things are in history, so the Liberals cannot proclaim themselves as the only champions of small businessmen, especially since they have ignored the plight of these small businessmen for so long.
The plight of the small businessmen is a matter of record. They have put themselves on record as being in need of relief from the provisions of the act that was passed by the Liberals, I believe in all sincerity, probably feeling that these provisions would cover certain aspects of the needs of that time. However, even they could not foresee all the implications. As some proof of this, I should like to quote a telegram received on June 24, 1959 from the president of the Retail Merchants Association of Canada. This was shortly after the bill was introduced last year. It is addressed to the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, Minister of Justice, House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario:
Whereas the Retail Merchants Association of Canada deeply appreciates your exhaustive research

Combines Investigation Act into the many problems besetting independent merchants and your sincere and earnest desire to help small business by your carefully prepared amendments to section 34 it is hereby resolved that a hearty vote of thanks be tendered to you, sir, and it is hoped that the consumer as well as the retailer will benefit by Bill 59-
