I have received letters from people in my own constituency suggesting that at this session of parliament we should eliminate the loss leader practice, predatory price cutting, discriminatory prices and false advertising, by enacting legislation. This letter is from Mr. A. J. Sone, who owns a corner drug store in my riding. Actually, it is in the riding of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), but his business extends into my riding. I also have a letter from Mr. Cushing, Mr. Bel-yea and from Van Wagner's (Toronto) Limited. These letters are some indication of the pressure on the government to make these changes. I have my office on a street on which there are many of these small businessmen, and as I visit them from time to time they are stressing the necessity for making these changes. In addition the Bloor district businessmen's association, of which I am a member, has been urging upon me the necessity for making these changes. All these people feel, as a result of their study, that these changes are necessary.
There was a pamphlet put out by the retail businessmen's association, and in referring to complaints that had been made to Canadian manufacturers as a result of loss leaders and so on being used by the larger combines, it stated:
Their hands are tied by a law passed by the Canadian parliament on December 31, 1951, the law being section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act. Among other things, section 34 prohibits any manufacturer from setting a minimum retail price for his own product, or refusing to supply his product to any retailer, however disagreeable he may find the retailer's abuse of the price of his product.
At first glance, the legislation would appear to be exactly what the doctor ordered from the point of view of the retail merchant, since it prevents a manufacturer from refusing to supply his product to a retailer who would otherwise be left on the outside looking in.
Further on it states as follows:
And it turns out to be a fact that Canadian retailers are far from satisfied with the legislation. Not long ago. Home Goods Retailing, a Maelean-Hunter publication, conducted a survey of retailers coast to coast. This paper, which serves retailers

in house furnishing, floor coverings, appliances, radio and television sets, lamps, furniture and housewares, published this report last September 3:
"A whopping 94 per cent of retailers who replied to this paper's queries on pricing said they favour a return to manufacturer-enforced retail prices, and 92 per cent agreed the present free-for-all price system is definitely harmful to business." ...
"The most overwhelmingly consistent reasons given as to why the present system is harmful (to the retailer) were based on these two points:
"1. It promotes consumer confusion which is destroying confidence in the retailer and the product.
"2. It is putting small retailers out of business through lack of profit."
I think that should definitely establish that there is a call, a requirement, by small businessmen for some change; and the change that is being suggested by the government is to try to meet that need.
I gathered the impression that perhaps there has been an overlooking of some of the aspects of this problem, in considering the problem from a somewhat three dimensional point of view, namely that of the producer or the supplier and the retail merchant and the consumer, and some are only looking upon the retail merchant as a mere funnel through which the producers' goods are distributed. In trying to prevent an entire monopoly by the various producers, however, I think that some have overlooked the problem of competition among the merchants themselves,' that is to say, the competition between the small merchant, the corner store merchant, the merchant in the ribbon areas as against the chain stores and some of the larger stores that have developed. These larger stores and chain stores through the means of loss leaders and so on have been making it more and more difficult for the small businessmen to survive. When some of these large chain stores make a loss leader of a product-and it was not always the same product and perhaps covers three or four or five products altogether-it heavily cuts into the products that are being sold by the various merchants.
There has also been that type of merchandising that has been carried on in the Toronto area-and perhaps in others-where someone organizes a large outlet. I give as an example the name of one we have had in the Toronto area, namely George's. They buy large quantities of electrical and other appliances and in many cases sell them for less than the price at which the manufacturer could sell them to the retailer, thus undercutting the whole market for that line of goods. Quite often I believe it is a matter of record that these companies stay in business for a very short time, often going into bankruptcy and owing their creditors a great deal of money. Somehow or other the money is got out of the

business but the damage to the business section in the economy is great, and in the long run is against the consumer's interest. Under the present legislation I understand the manufacturers feel that they cannot refuse to sell to these people without raising the presumption that they are price setting against the applicant. This is a situation that I think can be overcome by the present provision of the act.
I know that some of the C.C.F. members who have spoken have tried to ridicule the idea that we of the Conservative party would be trying to help the small businessman or even the corner store but I do not think they have any monopoly on the hopes and aspirations of the little people in this country.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate on this bill with very great interest and I have found it most instructive. The subject of anti-combines legislation is a difficult one. Our legislation itself has a far-reaching effect on the economy of the country, an effect which I think most objective students will agree is beneficial to the advancement of Canadian society and Canadians generally who comprise that society.
I was very much interested in the minister's presentation of the bill to the house on second reading. I was taken by his apparent attitude of being on the defensive throughout his presentation of the bill to the house, and particularly with his attempt to spend so much time defending the record of the Conservative party in this field over a number of years. His statement of the history of the matter omitted all the most important references to the records of parliament or of legislation throughout that period, although he was correct in his reference to the original date. I was curious about why he found it necessary to defend his party's history on this subject so strenuously. He had unlimited time but he chose to use his time for that purpose. I can only say that I hope students of this subject will look at the record and not take the minister's word as it stands without verifying it with the record over the years.
Throughout yesterday's debate on the bill we had a most interesting attitude revealed by the minister. He was creating the impression, at least on some of us, that he did not want the bill debated and he was interjecting regularly. No supporter of the government took any part. I am happy to see that today he has reformed. It is a very desirable reform. He has been patient in listening to the debate, and I hope he will find this small part of the debate of some constructive value

and of some interest. I am also glad to see that the supporters of the government have taken part in the debate on second reading. The bill warrants this because it is of sufficient importance to have all the examination and light which can be thrown on it by debate in the house.
It is very tempting to deal with the subject in a broad way; the whole subject of combines and anti-combines legislation is vast. Indeed I would like very much to deal with it but I think the time allocated to me can be more profitably used if I seek to examine the bill now before us in order to discern from the provisions of the bill what principles I think are involved and in what respects the bill modifies or repudiates principles in the anticombines legislation presently existing.
For the purpose of my argument I would like to recall to the house that the minister, as reported on page 4340 of Hansard, made it quite clear that the bill proceeds on the basis of the inherent soundness of the principles of the present anti-combines legislation; and he went on to say that the government believes that the principles of the legislation now in effect are sound. I am somewhat mystified, if he holds that view, why he went so far in changing those principles, because I hope to show in the course of my argument that that is precisely what he has done. Through this bill he has not done what he stated in the excerpts of his speech which I quoted; rather he has through the bill submitted something which if it is enacted will change the principles of the present legislation. With that in mind I will try to develop my argument.
First of all I think reference ought to be made to the principle to be found in clause 13 of the bill dealing with the changes in section 32 of the existing act. The principle, as I understand it from this part of the bill, is the principle of defining combinations and agreements-specifically setting them out- which are now being made legal. This will be found at the bottom of page 6 of the bill where six specific types of agreement subject to certain conditions are made legal. They include agreements for the exchange of statistics, the defining of product standards, the exchange of credit information, the definition of trade terms, co-operation in research and development, and restriction of advertising.
I think most hon. members will agree it is desirable that there should be co-operation in the development of research. The development of research in this country raises a real problem, many of our companies being too small to afford the necessary organization unless it is set up in combination. I have some doubt with regard to some of the other items 79951-0-280
Combines Investigation Act mentioned in that list, on the ground that these legal combinations as defined in this clause may open up an opportunity for a few persons or corporations who may be seeking to operate illegally to take advantage of this provision in order to develop combinations which would be offensive to the legislation.
However, that is not the main point I wish to make now. The point I wish to develop is that the minister, in providing that these specifically enumerated combinations should be legal, has not taken adequate steps to preserve and protect the public interest. There are many ways in which the hon. gentleman could have provided such protection. One of them would be to provide for registration of such agreements or combinations so that the director under the act would have the opportunity of examining the development of activities with regard to legal combinations. There are other methods, too. The method of registration is used in the United Kingdom, although I am aware that the legislation is different in principle from our own. But the point I am making here is that registration or some other method should be used with regard to these legal agreements or combinations for the purpose of enabling the director and other interested authorities to prevent these legal agreements being abused.
One other thing. The minister spoke about the uncertainty and difficulty experienced by certain corporations in knowing when they were doing something which might be illegal under the present act with regard to combinations. He spoke of the confusion that exists. Admittedly the legislation is difficult to interpret and determine. I am not specifically critical of the minister on that account. The act is that way, and while I think the present bill is worse, I am not expressly critical of the minister on that point. But if the minister had provided some means of protecting the public such as I have suggested, then in addition to preserving the interests of consumers he would have enabled the companies themselves to know with clarity whether their agreements or combinations were in the proper form under the act.
There is another point I wish to make, and one which concerns me greatly. It arises out of the new principle introduced in clause 17(4) of the bill. I think that for the purpose of developing my argument I should put the paragraph on record. It reads:
In any case where subsection (2) of section 31 is applicable the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of the province may in his discretion institute proceedings either by way of an information under that subsection or by way of prosecution.

Combines Investigation Act
In the legislation as it presently stands, offences are subject to prosecution. It is quite true that an additional remedy to the penalties provided under prosecution was provided for by way of a mandatory order or a restraining order. What is provided now, as I interpret clause 17(4), is a whole new principle, that is, the substitution of a different remedy at the wish of the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of the province concerned in any of the ten provinces. That raises several objectionable features.
First of all, there was some doubt expressed as to the right of the crown to take jurisdiction by way of mandatory or restraining proceedings, because they were civil, and the whole basis of the anti-combines legislation as I understand it, except those sections having to do with patents and customs, is that it is the enforcement of criminal law. That is the basis upon which the federal government gets its jurisdiction, as I understand it. If I am correct as to that, then this new provision raises the whole question as to the validity of the legislation we are now being asked to enact, and there is grave doubt about the constitutionality of this measure.
This is a point that should be dealt with, because it is no longer a criminal offence to do certain of the things set out under the act; it may only be the subject matter of civil proceedings by way of information commenced by the crown for a mandatory order or a restraining order. That is a very dangerous proposition because the destruction of anti-combines legislation through the adoption of this new principle, on the grounds that it is ultra vires could, as I think all hon. members will agree, be a very serious thing.
I do hope the minister when he replies to this debate will address himself to this point.
